analysis.one_liner: Suspends bee-killing neonicotinoid pesticides until the EPA proves they are safe for pollinators.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 73 House members, was referred to the Agriculture Committee in July 2013 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the EPA to suspend four neonicotinoid insecticides—chemicals used to coat seeds and spray crops—on plants that attract bees, unless the agency first completed a rigorous field study showing the pesticides would not harm honey bees, native bees, birds, or bats [S2][S3]. It would also have blocked any new registrations of those pesticides for those uses in the meantime, and required the Interior Department to monitor native bee populations and report to Congress and the public every year [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced after US beekeepers lost an average of 45.1% of their colonies in a single winter, and after the European Union had already suspended the most widely used of these chemicals on crops [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial beekeepers and the businesses that rent hives for pollination, whose losses had reached record levels; fruit, nut, and vegetable growers who depend on pollination services worth an estimated $20–30 billion a year in US agriculture; gardeners and the general public, who rely on one-third of North American food production that depends on bee pollination; and native ecosystems, including songbirds that can be killed by a single treated corn kernel [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Beekeepers, growers, and everyone who eats

how_it_helps.text: Would have suspended imidacloprid, clothianidin, thiamethoxam, and dinotafuran on bee-attractive plants, trees, and cereals within 180 days unless the EPA completed peer-reviewed evaluation and field studies covering chronic low-dose exposure and residue buildup proving the chemicals safe for pollinators.

Would have barred the EPA from issuing any new registrations of these pesticides for seed treatment, soil application, or foliar treatment on bee-attractive crops until that safety determination was made, closing the door on continued conditional approvals.
Would have required the Interior Department to regularly monitor native bee health and populations, investigate unusual bee die-offs, and publish an annual public report to Congress.
Responded to documented colony collapse: US beekeepers lost 45.1% of colonies in the 2012–13 winter, and USDA scientists estimated colony survival was too low to meet pollination demands of US crops.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of neonicotinoid insecticides, led by the companies holding the patents on the four named chemicals, would lose sales on seed treatments, soil applications, and sprays for bee-attractive crops. Corn, soybean, and cereal growers who plant neonicotinoid-coated seed as standard practice would face the cost and uncertainty of switching to alternatives while the EPA review was underway.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pesticide makers and farmers using treated seed

drawbacks.text: Farmers growing corn, soybeans, and cereals commonly rely on neonicotinoid-coated seeds as their main defense against early-season insect pests; an immediate suspension with a 180-day deadline would have forced them onto untested alternatives, and the bill included no transition period or phase-out schedule.

The bill directed suspension before the EPA's own review was complete, on the theory that the burden should sit with the pesticide maker rather than the bees; critics would argue that the EPA, not Congress, is positioned to weigh the full evidence, and that a legislative suspension of named chemicals is a blunt instrument compared with the regulatory process it bypasses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: pollination underpins roughly a third of North American food production, and one-third of managed honey bee colonies were being lost each winter. The main cost falls on a concentrated group—pesticide manufacturers and growers who use treated seed—rather than on consumers directly. The design weakness is that it suspended the chemicals by deadline rather than phasing them out as substitutes were identified, which put real adjustment pressure on commodity farmers. On balance, the bill targeted a narrow class of chemicals for uses specifically linked to pollinator harm, not agriculture broadly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee in August 2013; it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers, joined by Rep. Earl Blumenauer, introduced the bill on July 16, 2013, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.
On August 13, 2013, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Horticulture, Research, Biotechnology, and Foreign Agriculture.
No further action was taken for the remainder of the 113th Congress: the bill never left the subcommittee and never received a vote in the House or Senate.
The bill's cosponsor list grew to 73 members, 71 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but that support never translated into committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Neonicotinoid pesticide manufacturers kept their seed-treatment and spray market intact, and growers continued using treated seed without switching costs. Beekeepers, who lost an average of 45.1% of colonies in the 2012–13 winter, gained nothing from the bill's failure, and the EPA's restrictions on these chemicals did not come from this Congress.

for.name: John Conyers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to the House Agriculture Committee.

for.name: Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Joined Conyers in introducing the bill on July 16, 2013.

for.name: 71 House Democrats and 2 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors, building a 73-member bipartisan list of support.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Frank Lucas (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on August 13, 2013, and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled in the 113th Congress.

against.name: Neonicotinoid pesticide manufacturers
against.role: Makers of imidacloprid, clothianidin, and thiamethoxam, including Bayer and Syngenta
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on neonicotinoids in the US and internationally, disputing the science linking the chemicals to bee declines and challenging the European Union's suspension in court.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily one-sided: 71 of the 73 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Agriculture Committee, which held jurisdiction, took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have suspended their flagship products for seed treatment, soil application, and spraying on bee-attractive crops unless proven safe for pollinators, and blocked new registrations in the meantime. Their sales depend on the uses the bill targeted; ordinary people bear the pollination and ecosystem costs when the chemicals harm bees.

Hive losses averaged 45.1% in the 2012–13 winter and colony survival was estimated too low to meet US pollination demand; suspending the linked chemicals addresses the core of their business risk. Their health is also the public's, since they supply the pollination behind a third of North American food.

industries.industry: Corn, soybean, and cereal farmers using treated seed
industries.note: Neonicotinoid-coated seed is standard practice in commodity row crops, so an immediate 180-day suspension would have forced a costly shift to other pest controls. Farmers also depend on the bees these chemicals threaten, so their interest is genuinely two-sided.

Growers of almonds, apples, avocados, cranberries and similar crops depend on bee pollination, which the bill would protect; a few also use neonicotinoid sprays on their own fields. The pollination benefit overwhelmingly dominates for this group.
